Readable and Self-Trained: An OCR Engine Whose Networks Enter as Measured Terms

Michael Sharpe

An empirical study in the mlws‑ocr project, 2026

Working draft; figures from mlws-ocr v0.18.20 (17 October 2026), kept current as the engine improves. The first draft measured v0.18.16 (13 October); Table 3b keeps the clean sets' figures release by release.

In brief

mlws-ocr is an OCR engine for printed English documents, written to be read. It is a classic engine (connected components, a prototype classifier, a beam decoder with a dictionary) that self-trained networks join one at a time. Each network has to win on every evaluation set before it is kept. The engine was built in seven weeks by one person. Every network in it was trained in a home office, on public data, on a Mac and two gaming PCs. It uses no pre-trained weights and no vision or language foundation model.

What the paper reports:

  • The design. Seventeen stage slots. A contract under which every stage returns a new page together with pictures and numbers saying what it did. Four profiles over the one pipeline, from a feature engine with no network at all (pure) to one with thirteen small networks and seven fitted judges (neural-table). A network enters only as an extra term in a score, or as a candidate that a small fitted judge can choose. It never replaces the rule it competes with, so the classic engine is always still there to compare against.
  • The decoder that matters most. Every line is read twice: once by the classic decoder from segmented glyphs, and once by an ensemble of three 1.10M-parameter line readers from the whole grey strip. A 16-weight logistic judge then picks one reading per line. Over the classic reading, the readers are worth from 1.7 characters (DOE reports) and 1.9 (letters) to 13 (typescripts) on scanned pages, and 22 on forms. On whole pages the judge adds little beyond the readers alone: at most 0.2 characters and 1.1 words, and on the typescripts it costs half a character.
  • The comparison. We measured against both Tesseract engines with the same scripts on the same pages. On pages held out from our decisions, the neural profile leads both engines on letters, legal pleadings, newspapers and magazines. On two UNLV sets that the project had not opened before this paper, the picture changes. The first draft measured them at v0.18.16. On DOE technical reports the engine was level with the LSTM, and it still is (86.2 / 79.5 against 86.6 / 77.5). On annual reports it was 14 characters behind, because its layout read two-column pages straight across their narrow gutters. Four releases later, columns and statements are found without a hint, and the gap is 8 characters (77.9 against 86.1). Those releases were developed on other pages of the same report set, and §6.1 says what that does to the clean sets.
  • An audit of our own held-out claim. The "held-out" UNLV pages had been kept out of every layout and tuning decision, but not out of recognition training. The harvests that cut real text lines for the readers excluded only the evaluation draws. All 30 held-out letters, legal pages and newspaper pages, and 24 of the 30 magazine pages, had lent lines to training. The six magazine pages that had not are no remedy: they are the pages from which the harvest could match no line, so a page is among them because the engine read it badly. The honest clean test is a set that the harvests never opened. Since 13 October the harvests refuse the held-out pools, but the current readers still learn from lines cut before then.
Abstract

mlws-ocr is an OCR engine for printed English, written to be read: a classic pipeline of seventeen stage slots, each of which returns its result together with pictures and numbers saying what it did. Small networks trained by the project, from public data on home hardware, enter it under rules. Each network is a gated term in a score, or a second candidate that a judge of 16 to 32 fitted weights may choose, and the rule it competes with is never removed. Four profiles run over the one pipeline, from no network to thirteen.

The decisive network is a line reader, three of 1.10M parameters averaged, that reads each line's grey strip beside the classic decoder. Against the classic reading it is worth from 1.7 to 13 characters on scanned pages, and 22 on forms. The judge that chooses between the two readings adds at most 0.2 characters on whole pages, and removes about a tenth of the remaining errors on the lines where the readings differ.

Against both Tesseract engines on the same pages, the neural profile leads on 30-page samples of UNLV letters, legal pleadings, newspapers and magazines. Those pages were held out from every layout and tuning decision. An audit for this paper found that they were not held out from training: the readers had been trained on lines cut from them. On two UNLV sets that the project had not opened before this paper, the first draft (v0.18.16) found a mixed result: level with the LSTM engine on DOE technical reports, and 14 characters behind it on annual reports, whose two-column pages were read across their narrow gutters. At v0.18.20, after a column finder that needs no hint and a reading of financial statements by their figures, it is still level on DOE (86.2 against 86.6 pooled character accuracy) and 8 characters behind on the reports (77.9 against 86.1). That work was developed on other pages of the report set, but the measured pages have since informed one decision, though never training.

We report the audit, the clean results release by release, and the measurement faults found along the way. Most of them flattered the engine; one ran the other way.

1Introduction

Most OCR engines are now built in one of two ways. Some are pipelines whose recognizer is a long short-term memory network trained by connectionist temporal classification: Tesseract 4 and 5 [Smith 2007], OCRopus [Breuel et al. 2013], Calamari [Wick et al. 2020]. Others are end-to-end models pre-trained at scale that read a page straight to text: TrOCR [Li et al. 2023], Donut [Kim et al. 2022], Nougat [Blecher et al. 2023]. Both kinds are hard to read. The LSTM's decisions are one forward pass inside a page analysis that is itself decades of accreted code. The foundation model's decisions are a billion weights that nobody in the loop trained.

mlws-ocr takes a third route, chosen for legibility rather than for leaderboard position. It starts from a classic engine, the one Tesseract's legacy engine describes [Smith 2007], re-derived stage by stage with a debug rendering for each. Small networks are then admitted under four rules:

  1. Every network is trained by the project, from public data, on home hardware, and runs from one exported .npz in numpy.
  2. A network enters as a gated term in a score (a second opinion on a glyph's candidates, a rescoring of a word's segmentation variants), or as a second candidate that a fitted judge can choose. It never deletes the rule it competes with.
  3. A network is adopted only when it measures better on every evaluation set. Until then it is an option, off by default, and the project's owner decides each adoption.
  4. Every algorithm has a row in a research log naming its source and its measurement, including the ones that failed.

This paper describes the system that came out of that process seven weeks after its first commit, at release v0.18.20. Its first draft measured v0.18.16, and the clean sets are given release by release since then. Four companion papers cover particular parts of it in depth: the block segmenter [Sharpe 2026a, 2026b], the diagnosis method that found its largest defects [Sharpe 2026c], and table structure [Sharpe 2026d]. This paper covers the whole engine, how the networks fit into it, and what it measures against Tesseract. It also reports one thing the earlier papers got wrong: which pages were really held out.

The claims are a laboratory report. The engine is English only and seven weeks old, and every number in this paper is our own measurement, on sets we chose, with scripts we wrote. Section 9 says what that does and does not license.

2The stage contract

The pipeline is a fixed sequence of seventeen slots (Figure 1):

  • five for cleanup: magnify, deskew, illumination, binarize, despeckle;
  • five for layout: picture zones, rulings, blocks, ruled tables, lines;
  • six for recognition: components, recognize, decode, adapt, a second decode, correct;
  • one for output.

Each slot is filled by one registered implementation, for example deskew = projection or blocks = judged. An implementation is a class with a slot name, an implementation name and a defaults table that declares every parameter it accepts. Its one method takes a Page (grey image, binary image, resolution, and a metadata tree holding everything learned so far) and returns a new Page together with a DebugBundle: images, scalars and notes saying what the stage did. Two consequences carry the rest of the design:

  • Nothing is hidden. The command line writes every stage boundary of a run to disk: page image, page JSON, debug images, parameters and timing. A read-only viewer browses those runs. A workbench re-runs any stage live with changed parameters or a hand correction (a deskew angle, a speck, a block, a word), and shows each stage's pictures. A stage is not finished until a person can look at what it did.
  • Nothing is silent. A profile key that no stage declares is an error, so a misspelt parameter cannot do nothing. The evaluation scripts build the stage list with the same loader as the command line, so an evaluation and a run cannot disagree about what a profile is.

A profile is a TOML file that names an implementation and parameters for each slot. There are four, and a test fails if they differ anywhere except where this list says:

  • pure: the feature engine alone. No network: prototype matching, a beam decoder, a lexicon and character trigrams.
  • classic: pure plus two light networks (a 53k-parameter MLP second opinion on each glyph and a 258k-parameter character GRU language model) and a word corrector with a learned noisy channel. This is the reference engine. It never gains a network term, and after every adoption elsewhere it must reproduce its own figures.
  • neural: classic's recognition and decoding terms plus the line reader and its judge, a word-strip scorer, a word-confidence calibrator, a segmenter judge for newspapers and magazines, and an equation reader. It also switches on the table, picture and equation options.
  • neural-table: neural plus the table networks (a detector, a structure network, a separator network, a word-relation transformer, a table sequence reader, their choices and a cell confidence) and the readers trained for table crops.

3The classic engine

The classic engine follows Tesseract's legacy design [Smith 2007] closely enough that its documentation is also a readable account of that design, and departs from it where measurement said to.

Cleanup. The page is magnified when the type is small, deskewed by projection profiles, flattened by dividing out a median background, binarised by Sauvola's method [Sauvola & Pietikäinen 2000], and despeckled with a size threshold tied to the page's own x-height.

Layout. Picture zones are found by density and removed, and rules by morphology. Text blocks come from a recursive XY-cut [Nagy & Seth 1984] that is told the document type. On newspapers and magazines in the neural profiles, a 32-weight ridge judge instead chooses per page among four candidates: two XY-cuts and two variants of the directional k-NN strong-component segmenter [Sharpe 2026a, 2026b]. Lines come from projection profiles within each block. A line taller than 1.8 times the median is split again, against a reference that since v0.18.16 is capped by the size of the letters when most of a page's lines have fused.

On a page that arrives with no type, since v0.18.17 in the neural profiles the gutters of a whitespace-rectangle search [Breuel 2002] steer the XY-cut: columns are cut before rows where a gutter runs, and a page with two gutters is segmented as a newspaper. Since v0.18.20 a gutter's foot over a table or figure spanning the page is cut across first, beside prose columns only. In the output stage, a block of figures is read row by row with the label block whose lines share its baselines. That is the row step of T-Recs [Kieninger & Dengel 1998], keyed on the figures. Both changes came out of the clean test (§6.1).

Recognition. Connected components are grouped into glyphs, with alternatives for touching and broken characters. Each glyph gets up to 14 ranked candidates from three channels:

  • a condensed nearest-prototype library of 9,900 vectors over 95 features, built from renders of 35 open faces and real glyphs harvested from scans;
  • the MLP second opinion;
  • a re-derivation of Tesseract's outline-segment static classifier.

Decoding. A beam search per word runs over the candidates and the cut alternatives, scored by a lexicon, character trigrams and the GRU. The document then teaches the engine its own font (adapt): glyphs are clustered, pure clusters pin their members' labels, and a second pass decodes with the pins as a prior.

The neural-table profile adds the models for tables: a detector (248k), a structure network (277k), a separator network (44k), a word-relation transformer (321k), a table sequence reader (1.88M), a symbol classifier, three line-reader ensembles of the earlier 287k size fine-tuned on table lines and symbols, a cell confidence, and three fitted choices among the table builders. Its data is PubTables-1M and FinTabNet.c training tables and tables drawn by the project's own generator [Sharpe 2026d]. With every model counted, the neural profile carries about 4.8 million parameters, 3.3 million of them in the three line readers. The largest single network, neural-table's table sequence reader, has 1.88 million.

Three patterns recur, and each keeps the classic engine in the comparison:

  • A gated term. The MLP adds a disagreement cost to the prototype candidates. The character GRU adds a score to the beam. The word-strip CRNN scores each segmentation variant of a word by the CTC likelihood of its text. Switching any of them off leaves a working engine.
  • A second candidate and a fitted judge. The line reader proposes a whole line, and a logistic judge decides per line whether it replaces the classic reading (§5). The segmenter judge chooses among four block segmentations per page. In neural-table, three table builders compete with the rules' table, and a fitted choice keeps one per table. The judges are deliberately tiny (16 to 32 weights), fitted on harvests that are disjoint from the evaluation pages, and can be read off.
  • A new capability. The equation reader and the table networks add output the classic engine does not have (LaTeX and MathML for display equations; table structure). These sit behind options and are scored on their own sets.

Every network is trained from three kinds of public data:

  • renders made by the project: lines and windows set in open fonts through a degradation model; tables and pages drawn by generators with exact truth; formulas typeset by TeX;
  • real scans whose truth text lets lines be cut and labelled: the UNLV pages outside the evaluation draws, the training splits of SROIE and FUNSD, and Library of Congress pages transcribed by volunteers (the Historical Legal Reports typescripts and African American Perspectives in Print);
  • the PDF text of PubTables-1M and FinTabNet.c for tables.

A line reader trains from scratch in about four and a half hours on a consumer graphics card. The cards are run at half duty, so as not to run the home machines flat out for days.

5Two readers and a judge

The neural profile reads every text line twice (Figure 2).

The classic reading comes from the decoder of §3: segmented glyphs, their ranked candidates, a beam per word under the lexicon, trigrams and the GRU, and the word-strip CRNN rescoring each word's segmentation variants.

The line reader reads the line without segmenting it. The strip is cut from the flattened grey page (not the binary one), with any ruling that crosses it painted out, and contrast-normalised. A long strip is chunked at its widest gaps. The network is Shi, Bai and Yao's CRNN [Shi et al. 2017] shrunk to fit: four 3×3 convolutions (32, 64, 128 and 128 channels) that keep a column stride of 2 pixels, a bidirectional GRU of 192 units each way, and a linear layer to 112 classes with the CTC blank [Graves et al. 2006]. That is 1.10M parameters. Until v0.18.18 the reader had a quarter of the channels and half the GRU (287k). A pilot that varied only the size found the larger reader better by 0.2 to 1.4 words on every development set. It also found the reader limited more by its real data than by its size, so the larger readers came with a harvest of 49,865 real lines from two Library of Congress campaigns. They are trained from scratch, three seeds of one recipe, and averaged frame by frame. A CTC prefix beam search reads the averaged posteriors, with the lexicon as a word-level bonus. A reading whose mean emission probability is under 0.35 is declined, and the line keeps its classic reading.

The judge decides each line on which the two readings differ. It is a logistic regression with 16 weights over evidence that is cheap and symmetric between the readings:

  • the share of each reading's words that the lexicon or a numeric format vouches for, and the count of those it does not;
  • each reading's mean confidence;
  • their length ratio and word agreement;
  • the share of numeric words, and the number of words;
  • the reader's negative log-likelihood per character of both texts, and the gap between them;
  • whether the classic decoder rejected a word;
  • one fact about the page: the share of its classic lines with no vouched-for word at all. A form or a receipt reads near 1 and a letter near 0.

The judge was fitted on 4,000 pairs harvested from non-evaluation pages, read by the readers it judges (it is refitted whenever they change). Each pair's label is whether the reading has fewer character errors than the classic text against the truth line. With probability 0.5 or more, the reading replaces the classic words. Two fixed rules run first. When the reader's text is the classic text with characters deleted, and every classic word is vouched for, the classic line is kept, because the reader cannot have seen less ink than the classic decoder did. A line the reader declines whose classic words are unendorsed specks at half the page's x-height is dropped.

The reader's own likelihood is not the judge. It was tried first, and it prefers the reader's own text by construction. It measured worse on every set than a plain count of endorsed words.

The line reader carries the gain. Against the classic reading it is worth 0.9 characters on the rendered business documents, 1.7 to 1.9 on DOE reports and letters, 3 to 7 on legal pages, annual reports, newspapers and magazines, 13.0 on the typescripts and 22.0 on the forms. In words it is worth 3.4 to 22.1 points on the scanned sets and 27.0 on the forms. The classic column has not moved since the first draft on the held-out sets and the business documents, whose layout is unchanged. On them the larger readers add 0.2 to 0.8 characters and 0.6 to 2.2 words to v0.18.16's 287k reader. The classic column has moved on the sets read with no hint (DOE, reports, typescripts and forms), whose layout v0.18.17 and v0.18.20 changed.

The judge adds little on whole pages: 0.2 / 1.1 on letters, 0.2 / 1.0 on the business documents, and on the other scanned sets within 0.2 characters and 0.5 words of the reader alone. On the typescripts and the forms it costs 0.5 and 0.2 characters. The first draft explained a judge this weak by its history: it had been fitted on an earlier reader's pairs and kept when the readers changed. It has since been refitted twice, each time on 4,000 pairs read by the readers it now judges, and the result is the same. The readers alone would make nearly the same engine. The judge is kept because it decides each disagreement where the classic reading is strong, and because the next table shows what it does on the lines themselves.

On these lines the reader removes two thirds to three quarters of the classic decoder's errors. The judge removes a further 8 to 9% of what remains, which closes two fifths of the gap to the oracle on DOE and a fifth of it on the reports. It takes the reading on 94 to 95% of the lines, where the reading is better on 79 to 86%, and it agrees with the label on 83 to 88%. It is a judge that mostly defers. Its gains are real but small, and a better one has room: the oracle is 0.25 to 0.7 errors per 100 characters below it.

6Measurement

Metrics. A page's output text and its truth are normalised the same way:

  • quotes and dashes are folded;
  • a word broken across a line end is joined on both sides;
  • runs of rule characters (-----) are dropped.

Character accuracy is then 1 minus the edit distance over the truth's length, and word accuracy the same over words. Both are taken over the whole page in reading order, so a column read in the wrong order costs as much as a misread one. Bag-of-words recall and precision are reported beside them, because they separate reading from ordering. A set's figure is the mean over its pages. A page whose run crashes scores zero and is counted.

For the two clean UNLV sets the per-page mean is the wrong summary, and we report the pooled figure instead: errors summed over the set, divided by the truth's characters summed over the set. Many DOE pages are figures whose truth is only the caption. Every engine reads the axis labels as well, and a page with 12 words of truth and 300 characters of labels scores −860%. The per-page mean on DOE is +8% for the neural profile (−11% at v0.18.16) and +19% for the LSTM, and it says nothing about either.

Tesseract. Version 5.5.3 with --psm 3 (automatic page segmentation) and no other setting, run by scripts/eval_tesseract.py on the same pages with the same scoring:

  • LSTM is --oem 3 with Homebrew's English model;
  • legacy is --oem 0 with the tessdata repository's eng.traineddata, the model that still carries the pre-neural engine.

The document-type hint. The neural profile's layout takes a hint (letter, legal, newspaper, magazine) that sets the XY-cut's gaps and switches the segmenter judge on. The UNLV held-out rows are measured with their set's hint, which is the protocol every earlier figure used. Tesseract has no such input. Table 4 gives the same pages without the hint. The clean sets and the external sets are measured with no hint.

Sets.

  • Clean (no training, and before v0.18.17 no decision; §6.1): DOE technical reports (doe3.3B) and annual reports (rep.3B), 30 pages each.
  • Held out from decisions (§6.1): 30 UNLV pages per type, seed 5.
  • Same collection as training, disjoint pages: 60 business documents rendered by the project's generator at a seed it was never trained at; 40 Library of Congress typescripts transcribed by volunteers (Legal Reports), whose readers were trained on other pages of the same campaign; the 50 FUNSD test forms [Jaume et al. 2019], with the training split used for training.

The evaluation draws (dev-8, broad-30, legal-8, news-8, mag-8) are not reported here. They were looked at for seven weeks while the engine was tuned.

6.1Which pages were held out

The project keeps three kinds of UNLV page apart, and checking them for this paper showed that one of the separations was weaker than its documentation said.

  • Evaluation draws. Thirty pages per set, drawn with seeds 1 and 2, give dev-8, broad-30, legal-8, news-8 and mag-8. Every harvester reproduces these draws and excludes them, together with the rescans of the same documents (bus.3A, news.4B). No training line or glyph has ever come from them. They were, however, looked at for seven weeks while the engine was tuned.
  • Decision pools [Sharpe 2026b]. Of the remaining pages, 30 per set were set aside for tuning the segmenters and 40 for training the segmenter judge. The rest form the held-out pool, from which seed 5 draws the 30 "held-out" pages per type. No layout or tuning decision has used the held-out pool.
  • Recognition harvests. The harvests that cut real lines, words and glyphs for the readers, and the pairs for the judges and calibrator, exclude only the evaluation draws. They predate the decision pools, and nobody made them exclude the held-out pool once it existed.

So the held-out pages were held out from decisions but not from training. Counting the pages of each held-out draw that appear in any harvest file, both those on the development machine and the grey-strip harvests on the training machines:

setpagesharvested for trainingheld-out poolof it, never harvestedheld-out 30, never harvested

The project's README had described these pages as ones "no tuning, training or evaluation decision has used", and two of the companion papers said the same [Sharpe 2026b, 2026c]. Tuning and evaluation were right; training was not. The README and both papers now say so. On these pages the line reader has seen the very text lines it is asked to read, cut from the same scans and labelled with their truth. Tesseract was trained on none of them.

Two UNLV sets had never been opened by this project before this paper: doe3.3B (785 pages of Department of Energy technical reports) and rep.3B (300 pages of reports). Both come from the same ISRI collection and the same scanning regime [Rice et al. 1996]. We fetched them for the first draft of this paper and measured them once, 30 pages each (seed 5), with no document-type hint and the engine frozen at v0.18.16. Nothing was changed before that result was written down.

What happened next has to be told, because it changes what the two sets are. The first draft's result pointed at the layout, and the next releases worked on it:

  • v0.18.17: columns found without a hint. This was developed on 60 other annual-report pages, drawn from rep.3B outside the measured 30, and on the newspaper and magazine decision pools. The measured 30 of both sets were read once more at the end, and that reading was before the project's owner when the change was adopted. From then on the two sets have informed one decision. They are still clean of training.
  • v0.18.18 and v0.18.19: larger line readers, then readers that learn the receipts without case. These were decided on the other sets. The clean sets were measured after each decision, and decided nothing.
  • v0.18.20: report sections and financial statements read in their order. Developed on the same 60 other report pages. The measured 30 were read once, after the decision.

So since v0.18.17 the clean sets are clean of training and of development, but not of every decision. Table 3b gives their figures release by release. The v0.18.16 row remains the one measurement taken before any decision had seen them.

The harvests have also changed. Since 13 October they refuse the held-out pools and the clean sets whole, in every scan of a document. The current readers still learn from the real lines harvested before that, so the audit table above still describes them. The next reader trained only on guarded harvests will be the first whose held-out pages are held out from training too.

The clean sets. These two rows are the only ones on pages that no training has touched. On the DOE reports the neural profile is level with both Tesseract engines: 0.4 characters behind the LSTM and 2.0 words ahead of it. Its median page reads 90.3% of characters, against the LSTM's 90.5%. On the annual reports it is 8.2 characters and 7.7 words behind, and its median page 87.8% against 95.1%.

At v0.18.16 the reports were 14 characters behind. The reason was mostly layout, not reading. Many of these pages set their text in two columns separated by a narrow gutter, and with no document-type hint the XY-cut read straight across both columns. Table 3b follows the two sets through the four releases since. Two of them were layout releases. v0.18.17 lets the gutters of a whitespace-rectangle search steer the XY-cut on a page with no type. v0.18.20 reads a two-column section before the table spanning the page beneath it, and a financial statement row by row by its figures.

Table 3b. The clean sets release by release, neural profile, pooled character / word accuracy (%). Each row was measured after that release's decision, except v0.18.17, whose measured reading was before the owner when it was adopted (§6.1).

v0.18.16the first draft; nothing decided on these sets85.9 / 78.172.2 / 68.4
v0.18.17columns found without a hint85.5 / 77.874.8 / 72.7
v0.18.18line readers of 1.10M parameters86.0 / 78.874.8 / 72.7

The layout releases moved the reports, by 2.6 and 2.9 characters; the reader releases moved DOE, by 0.8 in all, after v0.18.17 had cost it 0.4. On the reports neither layout release is a clean gain page by page. v0.18.17 fixed the worst page of the first draft (9500_034, 30.3% to 99.6%, level with the LSTM), but it cuts another into bands across its two columns, which are now read in alternating pieces (9529_025, 98.0% to 49.2%). v0.18.20 moved 12 pages, nine of them up by 2 to 33 points and one, 9561_026, down by 1.1.

The gap that remains is still mostly order. On the 21 report pages where the neural profile reads 90% or more of the truth's words, it scores 82.1% of characters on the mean page, against the LSTM's 91.8% (19 pages, 78.3% against 91.1%, in the first draft). Four of them are read 38 to 53 points below the LSTM with 92% or more of their words found. One further page is printed in reverse video (white type on black): every mlws-ocr profile still returns nothing for it, and the LSTM reads 84%.

Would the hint have saved the reports? Annual reports are no type the engine knows, so in the first draft we tried the nearest, the magazine hint, after seeing the result (Table 4). It raised the pooled figure only to 73.7 / 69.3, and moved 13 pages down and 6 up. Now that the layout finds the report columns itself, the hint costs 3.9 characters (74.0 / 70.1). The newspaper and magazine settings were tuned for other gutters.

The pages held out from decisions. Here the neural profile leads both engines on all four types, by 1.1 to 6.0 characters over the LSTM. Its readers were trained on lines from these very pages (§6.1), so this is a weaker claim than it looks. It is the claim earlier versions of this project made, and we keep the row so the two can be compared. Set beside the clean rows, it shows what the overlap is worth. Letters and DOE reports are both single-column office documents, and on them the gap to the LSTM is +1.1 with the overlap and −0.4 without it (+0.7 and −0.7 at v0.18.16). The comparison is loose, because the sets differ in more than the overlap.

We also checked the six held-out magazine pages that no harvest had used. There the neural profile reads 82.1 / 70.9 (79.8 / 63.1 at v0.18.16) and the LSTM 90.7 / 87.5. These pages are not a fair sample. The harvests processed them and kept no line from them, because no line of the engine's reading matched the truth closely enough. A page is in this subset because the engine read it badly. A clean subset defined by the training harvests inherits their selection, and the only honest clean test is a set the harvests never opened.

Same collection as training. On the rendered business documents the LSTM reads 97.8% of the words but scores 71.5% of characters. The documents are invoices, statements and payslips laid out in label and value columns. The truth follows the generator's own reading order, a convention the project's layout agrees with because the generator was built beside it. The row measures agreement with that convention as much as reading. The Library of Congress pages are typescripts from a volunteer transcription campaign, and the readers were trained on other pages of the same campaign. The LSTM is 10.4 characters behind on them, and the legacy engine 31.7. On FUNSD forms the neural profile leads the LSTM by 1.4 characters, and the two are level in words (47.0 against 47.2; at v0.18.16 the LSTM led by 2.2 words).

The hint is worth 2.3 and 3.1 characters on letters and legal pages, and 6.6 and 12.9 on newspapers and magazines. In the first draft it was worth 18.3 and 15.1 on the last two. The difference is v0.18.17's gutters, which take a page of no type with two gutters for a newspaper. That change was developed on the newspaper and magazine decision pools, not on these pages. Without the hint the neural profile still trails the LSTM on held-out newspapers and magazines, by 4.8 and 6.9 characters (16.8 and 9.8 in the first draft). The segmenter judge is worth 4.8 and 5.9 characters on top of the hint. So the layout's inputs still matter more on multi-column pages than any network in the recognizer. The hint is a fact about the document that a caller usually knows, but Tesseract gets no such fact, and on a page of unknown type the engine must guess. It now guesses well enough to read the clean reports' columns better than any hint it has, but not as well as Tesseract's page analysis does unprompted.

Tables and equations. Tesseract has no table structure and no equation output, so there is nothing to put beside these figures. In neural-table, held-out PubTables-1M crops score 0.879 TEDS-Struct / 0.940 TEDS and held-out FinTabNet.c crops 0.881 / 0.930 (240 tables each) [Sharpe 2026d]. The equation reader writes display equations as LaTeX and MathML. On 60 fresh typeset pages, 86.1% of equations are exact and 97.3% of tokens are right.

8What the measurements taught

The research log records many more failures of measurement than of mechanism. A system paper is the place to list them, because each one would have changed a decision if it had not been caught.

  • The evaluator crashed and the mean went up. One early measurement credited a change with eight word points on the typewriter set. A crash had dropped the pages the change made worse, and the mean was taken over the pages that remained. Every evaluation now reports its page count, and the count is checked.
  • An image loaded at the wrong scale. A figure script read a page as 0–255 instead of the engine's 0–1, and the segmentation it drew silently changed. One figure in an earlier paper was wrong until it was redrawn. Ad hoc scripts now load through the engine's own loader.
  • A script default overrode a profile. The equation evaluator's --beam defaulted to 1 and so overrode the profile's beam of 8. A release looked as though it did not reproduce its own figures until the two command lines were compared.
  • A judge that never judged. For its first days the fitted line-choice judge decided nothing. An if/elif chain had no branch for its rule name, so control fell through to the older fixed rule. It was caught when three different judges gave identical numbers. Each rule now returns its own decision, and an identical result from different models is treated as a symptom.
  • Conventions are worth points. The UNLV truth keeps a word broken at the end of a line as two halves, while the engine joins them. Scoring one convention against the other cost two word errors per wrapped word, four word points on news-8, for every engine. The evaluator now folds both. A set of born-digital pages had its truth in the PDF's stream order rather than visual order, and scored every engine about 50% for reasons that had nothing to do with recognition.
  • The protocol includes the hint. The neural profile takes a document-type hint (letter, legal, newspaper, magazine). A held-out run without it looks like a regression of up to eighteen points. Table 4 reports the profile both with and without the hint, because Tesseract gets no hint.
  • Eight pages flatter. At the end of September the engine read news-8 at 95.8% and 30 held-out newspaper pages at 79.7%. On a further 40 pages from the same set, XY-cut alone read 87.6%. Page-to-page variance on newspapers is larger than most of the changes being measured. Every adoption since has been confirmed on 30 or more pages that the change was not developed on.
  • Overlap hides in the metadata. Fine-tuning the line reader on receipts raised SROIE by 14 characters on the 44 evaluation receipts from shops that also appear in the training split, and by 8.7 on the 16 from new shops. No receipt was in both splits, but the shops were. The held-out pages of §6.1 are the same mistake one level up: no page was in two pools, but the pools were defined for one kind of decision and the harvests served another.
  • A clean subset inherits its definition's bias. The first attempt at a clean test took the held-out pages that no harvest had used. On magazines it found six, and on them the engine trailed the LSTM by 11 characters. Those six had been processed by the harvests and yielded no line, so they had been selected by the engine's own failure. The clean test became two sets that the harvests never opened.
  • A per-page mean can say nothing. On DOE reports the per-page mean char accuracy was −11% for the neural profile at v0.18.16, +8% now, and +19% for the LSTM. Pages that are a figure with a caption carry a dozen words of truth, and both engines read the axis labels too. The pooled figure (85.9 then, 86.2 now, against 86.6) is the measurement.
  • A disjointness asserted, not checked. The first draft's Table 2b said its 30 report pages were not the 30 of Table 2. Three of them were: the judge's harvest shuffles a set with its own seed and was never told which pages the measured draw holds. The table in this draft draws its pages with both the measured draw and the development pages left out, and checks it.
  • A label convention can teach a fault. The larger readers of v0.18.18 read whole lines of a degraded synthetic Verdana page in capitals. No real evaluation set showed it; the regression test on that page caught it. Four trainings looked for the cause in the typefaces: a second round with Google Fonts lines, a curriculum, distillation, and lighter receipt weights. The cause was a label. SROIE transcribes every receipt in capitals, and measured by letter heights, 22 of 24 evaluation receipts have lines printed in mixed case ('Cash Bill … Goods Sold are non-refundable'). Its 30,323 box lines had taught the reader that a small 'e' is read 'E'. The readers now learn those lines as partial labels [Cour et al. 2011]: before the loss each small letter's probability is added to its capital's, so the receipts teach their letters but not their case. The same convention scores a reader that keeps the print's case as wrong. SROIE fell from 63.4 to 48.5 words as scored, and held level with case folded (72.5 to 72.6). The evaluator now prints both.

Most of these faults made the engine look better than it was, or made a change look better than it was. An evaluator's errors are not symmetric: the ones that flatter survive, because nobody goes looking for them. The receipts' capitals ran the other way. The truth's convention made the reader that read the print correctly score worse, and the reader that had learned the convention's fault score better. What showed it was a synthetic page, whose truth follows no convention but the text.

9Limits

  • English, printed, and scanned or rendered. No other language has been tried. Handwriting is not read (the forms' hand-filled fields are read as well as a print reader can read them). Photographed receipts are out of scope until a profile of their own exists.
  • Our sets, our scripts, our pages. Every figure is the project's own measurement. The sets are small (8 to 60 pages), and a set of 30 pages moves by a point or more with the choice of pages. The clean sets of §7 are 30 pages each.
  • Tuned while measured, trained on the held-out pages. Seven weeks of decisions were taken on the evaluation draws. The held-out pools guard against that for layout decisions but, as §6.1 shows, not for the readers' training. The two clean sets are 60 pages in all, and since v0.18.17 they have informed one decision.
  • Forms. On FUNSD the engine leads the LSTM by 1.4 characters and is level in words; a form is still read at two thirds of its characters by either.
  • The layout still does best when told. Multi-column pages read best with the document-type hint, and only for the types it names. Without it the engine now finds the columns of newspapers and annual reports itself, but still trails the LSTM by 5 to 7 characters on held-out newspapers and magazines, and by 8 on the clean annual reports. A page of unknown type is the common case outside a laboratory.
  • Reverse video. A page printed white on black reads as nothing. The table profile inverts light text on a dark ground inside a table. For the text pipeline an inversion of white-on-black lines exists as an option, off. It reads the clean report page (0 to 96%), but it cost a held-out magazine page 36 points, and it stays off until pictures can be kept out of it on binary scans.
  • Speed. A page takes from a few seconds to about fifteen on one core, in numpy. The engine was written to be read, not to be fast.

10Conclusion

A classic OCR engine can be the frame for small networks without disappearing into them. Every network in mlws-ocr enters as a measured term or as a judged candidate. Every stage can be looked at. The classic profile still reproduces its own figures after each network is adopted elsewhere. What the frame buys is legibility: when the engine is wrong, a person can find out at which stage and why. Several of the largest single gains came from that rather than from bigger networks. A deskew estimate that had rotated magazine pages by five degrees was found by looking, and so were newspaper columns whose lines had fused (held-out magazines +5.0 characters, newspapers +2.4).

What it does not buy is a guarantee about pages it has not seen. On the pages held out from our decisions, the engine leads Tesseract on every type. On pages it had truly never seen, at v0.18.16, it was level on single-column technical reports and 14 characters behind on two-column annual reports. Part of the difference is the training overlap this paper found. Part was a layout that needed to be told what kind of document it was reading, and that on report pages found no columns even when told. The first draft named three next steps. Two are done:

  • a column finder that works without a hint, on the narrow gutters of report pages as well as on newspapers (v0.18.17 and v0.18.20; the reports 14 characters behind, now 8);
  • harvests that refuse every held-out pool and both clean sets (since 13 October), so that the held-out number of the next reader trained only on them will mean what it says.

The third, reverse-video text, is an option not yet safe to adopt. The reports point to what comes next:

  • statements whose labels wrap onto a second line, which the row step by figures does not yet join;
  • the report pages still read in pieces with nearly all their words found (§7), among them 9529_025, which v0.18.17 broke;
  • a reader trained only on guarded harvests.
